Flipper Zero vs. Flipper One: Why the new model isn’t an upgrade

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I missed the Flipper Zero Kickstarter in 2020, and I didn’t get my hands on one until 2023.
  • Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.
  • According to recent reports, just when I thought I’d reached the limits of what the Zero was capable of, I discovered the world of third-party firmware, which opened the door to even more features and tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I missed the Flipper Zero Kickstarter in 2020, and I didn’t get my hands on one until 2023. Since then, it’s been one of those devices that continually exceed my expectations. It’s the perfect gadget for making the unseen world of point-to-point access-control protocols visible, including sub-GHz radio, NFC, 125kHz RFID, infrared, and iButton. The stuff Flipper calls “Layer 0.”.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

According to recent reports, just when I thought I’d reached the limits of what the Zero was capable of, I discovered the world of third-party firmware, which opened the door to even more features and tools. Over the years, that scene has grown into an active community of developers building all sorts of novel apps for the platform.

Recent findings suggest that by May 2026, Flipper had sold over a million Zero units, and a large community had gathered around the device. When the tech giant introduced the Flipper One, it made it clear it wasn’t a replacement, but a totally new device. Comparing the two is like comparing a hammer to a screwdriver, so what are the major differences?

The Flipper One is a full Linux computer (running the Debian-based Flipper OS on a mainline Linux kernel) built to work with everything that’s IP-connected: Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and, via M.2 expansion modules, 5G and satellite. If you wanted, you could use the One as a router, a VPN gateway, or a bridge between wired and wireless networks — so-called “layer 1” stuff.

The Zero is one of those rare devices that continually managed to exceed my expectations. It was a small, pocket-sized gadget that made visible the unseen world of point-to-point access-control protocols such as sub-GHz radio, NFC, 125kHz RFID, infrared, and iButton.

I’ve lent my Zero to youngster, and within a few minutes they’re using it to do real stuff, and they’re learning as they go. Everything is built-in, and Flipper the Dolphin (took me a while to get that) is there to guide you through the steps.

You could easily spend six months running the software on the Zero and working your way through the Lab, Flipper’s free app store, before you’re ready to delve into the third-party firmware options out there.

Also: Heat from your charger could be killing your battery – I found one that stays cool.

According to recent reports, and thanks to Flipper selling over a million units, that third-party scene has grown into an active community of developers building all sorts of novel apps for the platform. When you’re ready to make that leap, I suggest starting with Unleashed. This will give you the familiarity of the firmware that came with the Flipper Zero, but add features — such as extending the sub-GHz frequency range by removing geolocation blocks and adding a lot of NFC-related features, and fun things like games.

It has been revealed that you can pick up a Zero now for $169 and be using it to explore the world around you by the end of the week. I’m not saying don’t jump on the Kickstarter and get a One for the special price of $399 (especially considering that once it’s out, it’ll retail for $550), but that unit won’t be in your hands until at least July 2027.

The One is a very different beast to the Zero. While the Zero runs FreeRTOS-based firmware, the One is a full computer powered by the Debian-based Flipper OS on a mainline Linux kernel. This means that the One can have USB, HDMI, and Ethernet ports, and like a PC, it’s expandable thanks to the M.2 slot which supports SSD drives and optional radio modules.

You can even connect a One to a keyboard and external display for a full desktop experience.

While the Zero is the tool for point-to-point access-control protocols where there’s no network, no IP addresses, and no internet involved, the One is for everything IP-connected, such as Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and, by making use of optional M.2 modules, 5G, LoRa, and satellite. This means that you can customize the One to be a network appliance such as a router, VPN gateway, or a bridge between wired and wireless networks.

Also: Flipper Zero: ‘Can you really hack Wi-Fi networks?’ and other questions answered.

Sources indicate that being a full computer also means the Wi-Fi will be more capable and fully featured than the Wi-Fi on a laptop. Anything that you can do on a computer, you can do with the One.

Flipper’s aim with the One is “to create a fully upstream-supported ARM computer that never becomes outdated.” To achieve this, Flipper is putting its drivers into mainline Linux rather than building a custom kernel. The One should continue to get kernel updates for a long time to come. But as of right now, the software is unfinished, and it has been asking the community to help finish drivers and core software.

It’s worth pointing out that some have their doubts that Flipper will be able to achieve its goal of no binary blobs, no proprietary drivers, and no vendor-locked board support package, and that there will still be some for things like Wi-Fi and cellular connectivity.

Here’s a comparison chart detailing the differences between the two.

According to recent reports, I wish I could simply recommend one over the other, but it’s not that kind of choice. The real question is whether you need “Layer 0” or “Layer 1” tools, not which Flipper is “better”. You might decide you need both. Full disclosure: I haven’t gotten my hands on a One yet, and the question is — can Flipper make it easy to use?

The Zero wasn’t a success because it was powerful, it was a success because it made an invisible world fun and easy to explore for a relatively small price tag and with almost no learning curve.

Also: I’ve owned 50+ portable power stations – one number matters most for its lifespan.

The One has been made to a different script. It’s more than twice the price; it’s bulkier, a full Linux machine with a learning curve to match, and you’ll need modules (and probably an external display) to get the most out of it. If Flipper can make network tinkering as friendly as the Zero made radio, it’ll be a hit. If it can’t… well, the One becomes yet another mini-PC. And this question can’t be answered until the One ships.

One thing’s for sure, I can’t wait to get my hands on it.

Copilot is "the upcoming OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its latest “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.
  • Industry observers note that the announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software.
  • Recent findings suggest that the rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the organization first announced in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its latest “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”.

Industry observers note that the announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the latest Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

Recent findings suggest that the rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the organization first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.

It has been revealed that copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that consumers can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.

Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

In a recent development, copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment at the moment available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”.

Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s upcoming frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he mentioned.

In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft claims each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

Sources indicate that the promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the tech giant’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure must still be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will need to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Sources indicate that along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and MasterCard, to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”.

Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The upcoming agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”.

Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”.

According to recent reports, nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he noted. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”.

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure plan.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been on a quest to minimize my dependence on my Android phone. It started with blocking sensitive information from appearing on my lock screen. The next step was turning off notifications on my lock screen completely. I started feeling more at ease throughout the day. I no longer felt the pull to pick up my phone to see if someone had replied to something, if something happened in the news, or if I missed social media posts.

Industry observers note that then I considered my Android phone’s home screen launcher, which is the window to our mobile digital world. I’d already switched from the default Pixel launcher to Mango Launcher, which I was enjoying and which slightly lessened the distractions. But could a more minimal launcher bring me even more peace?

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

Recent findings suggest that I’d already tried AIO Launcher, and found it to be one of the coolest minimal launchers that I’d ever tried. Then I found three that are even better: Ying Yang Launcher, Olauncher, and Indistractable Minimalist Launcher.

Yin Yang Launcher aims to help you use your phone less, and it does a remarkable job. With Yin Yang Launcher, your Android screen is replaced with two options: basic and minimal. The minimal option is what I chose to focus on, as it breaks the Android display into four pages:.

According to recent reports, if you swipe down from the center of the display, you get a search page, where you can search for installed apps or search the web. Of course, if you swipe down from the top, you get the standard Android Notification Shade.

Sources indicate that long-press the main page to access the settings, where you can customize the home screen, appearance, launcher settings, system settings, and the Mind Space. The Mind Space is a unique feature that serves as a focus mode, where you can select which apps to use and set focus schedules. You can also trigger a manual focus mode and set how long it lasts and which apps are allowed. If you purchase the Pro version of Yin Yang Launcher, you can enable strict mode, which means you cannot disable focus mode until the set time elapses.

Just using Yin Yang Launcher gives me a sense of peace that no other launcher offers.

Also: Changing these 12 settings on my Android phone extended its battery life by hours.

Sources indicate that yin Yang Launcher is free to install from the Google Play Store. There is also a Pro version that adds more features and removes ads. The Pro version is $14.99/yr or $29.99/lifetime.

I’ve written about Olauncher before. It’s similar to Yin Yang Launcher, without the extra features. With Olauncher, you get a home page with the apps you choose to list; a right swipe opens the phone app, a left swipe opens the camera app, a swipe up opens the full list of apps, and a swipe down opens the Notification Shade.

Long-press the home screen to gain access to the Olauncher Settings, where you can customize the appearance, gestures, the number of apps on the home screen, and a few more options.

Olauncher is about as minimal as it gets. If you want more, you can purchase the Pro version, which adds features like weather, widgets, fonts, folders, AMOLED wallpapers, and more. Presently, Olauncher Pro is still in early access, so you can use it for free.

In a recent development, indistractable Minimalist Launcher is all about digital detox, and it does a great job with it. You get a text-based layout that lists the time and date, the year and day in progress, your calendar, and a text-based app launcher list of favorites you set.

Sources indicate that that’s the long and short of Indistractable Minimalist Launcher, and for anyone looking for a complete digital detox, this is what you want. Indistractable Minimalist Launcher looks like a throwback to an older age of computing, and that’s intentional. If you want the absolute bare minimum, with no distractions, install this launcher.

Right now, Indistractable Minimalist Launcher is in early access, so it’s free to install and use from the Google Play Store.

As for my current minimalist launcher of choice, I prefer Yin Yang Launcher for phones and the aforementioned AIO Launcher for tablets.

Latest Update: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA.
  • MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning.
  • Sources indicate that “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.

MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

Sources indicate that “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”.

In an accompanying announcement video, Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”.

Wright remarked MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

Since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”.

Recent findings suggest that but Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi, a mobile simulation that was first announced in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.

Now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency. Until now, that manufacturer has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.

Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing says the company’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to major tech surveillance.

It has been revealed that “Meta knows what you click,” the company writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”.

According to recent reports, wright stated the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research manufacturer” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.

“Right now AI has opened a vast newly introduced design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright mentioned.

Of the four tweeters, one forward-firing mid-tweeter handles center audio, while two side-firing tweeters and one up-firing tweeter create separation and height, critical for directional audio in Dolby Atmos playback.

Industry observers note that also: Sonos Era 300 vs. Denon Home 400.

It has been revealed that the Era 300 works amazingly in a pair, connected to a powerful soundbar like the Arc Ultra. However, you have the freedom to set up one or multiple around your home as standalone speakers. The Era 300 is also fitted with a microphone for voice assistant support and Trueplay room acoustic tuning, though you can toggle the mic off at any time via a physical switch.

Recent findings suggest that the Arc Ultra is Sonos’ latest and most capable flagship soundbar, with 15 Class-D amplifiers powering nine tweeters and six midwoofers. Two tweeters fire upward for immersive audio height channels, while the others are angled along the Arc Ultra’s horizontal frame for dialogue and high frequencies. The Arc Ultra’s most amazing feature is its built-in woofer, which delivers a clearly felt and heard bass response. You could hold off on a Sonos Sub for a while if you go with the Arc Ultra.

Recent findings suggest that the Roam 2 sports a 10-hour battery and an IP67 durability rating. Despite its small size, I actually recommend it only to the most dedicated Sonos fans, as there’s little return on investment if you don’t already have several Sonos speakers. The Roam 2 isn’t a speaker you build a system around.

Recent findings suggest that the Move 2 is the most advanced Wi-Fi/Bluetooth hybrid speaker in Sonos’ lineup, with three Class-D amplifiers, two tweeters, and one midwoofer to back it up. This speaker’s acoustic structure is identical to that of the Era 100, so if you don’t need the Move 2’s portability, go with the Era 100.

The Move 2 is humidity-resistant, so it’s not suited for splashes or accidental falls in water. Additionally, it weighs 4.3 pounds, so it’s not the best option for fast-paced adventures. The Move 2 is, however, a very solid choice for someone who wants a capable Sonos speaker they can easily move from room to room, or from the kitchen to the patio.

Industry observers note that sonos doesn’t put its speakers on sale often and generally doesn’t offer the most eye-popping deals, either. However, it’s rare for the entire Sonos catalog to be on sale, so this year’s Black Friday sale is a great time to buy multiple speakers if you want to add a few more components to your system.

Industry News: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
  • When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
  • Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.

Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.

“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”.

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”.

According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”.

Industry observers note that raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output noted, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Sources indicate that at least one staffer noted they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with people in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member remarked the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”.

Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

Sources indicate that but Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the concerns the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving people other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”.

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse people in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten remarked was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.

But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”.

According to recent reports, around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.

Sources indicate that “I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”.

According to recent reports, it seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton stated. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”.

Industry observers note that “We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”.

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.

Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

Industry observers note that but staffers warned Meta that consumers may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

Meta says that Muse customers can trust the organization to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant mentioned it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

Industry observers note that on iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta rolled out Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

According to recent reports, part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”.

In a recent development, apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to owners complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

“We are committed to ensuring customers understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

#21746. Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home.
  • Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat.
  • The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.

In a recent development, at least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.

Recent findings suggest that “No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”.

In a recent development, only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.

“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly stated. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”.

The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.

Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.

The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.

Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—said that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”.

The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.

“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt mentioned. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”.

All the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.

In a recent development, car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, stated his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”.

Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.

Industry observers note that “The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield said. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”.

The teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.

Recent findings suggest that in a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.

The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.

They also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG remarked.

Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”.

Industry observers note that another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.

In a recent development, these recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.

“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.

The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.

It has been revealed that BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.

Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.

Sources indicate that “What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”.

Mitchell said that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.

“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell stated. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”.

Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”.

“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang said.

Industry observers note that as a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she stated.

Sources indicate that “I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield mentioned. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”.

According to recent reports, kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”.

According to recent reports, as AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release remarked. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”.

Also: The best smartwatches of 2026: Expert tested and reviewed.

In a recent development, our no. 1 most-purchased smartwatch is a screenless fitness tracker with a seven-day battery life and a discreet look that blends in with whatever you wear. It’s an easy wearable to keep on, thanks to its week-long battery life and the fact that it looks more like a bracelet than a health tracker.

The Fitbit Air is comfortable to work out with and sleep with, something I can’t say about many smartwatches that do the same thing (for double the price). Google’s Health app is one of my favorites, with an engaging interface that displays weekly cardio capacity, sleep score, readiness, and other metrics right at the top, where I want them. The Fitbit Air is $100 without any promotion tacked on — a good deal already on a near-perfect product.

Sources indicate that even though the Apple Watch Series 11 is a year old, it’s still an excellent buy. In fact, this year’s Series 12 has the exact same battery life as the Series 11 (24 hours), and most of the upgrades to the Series 12 come through latest Audio Intelligence features and sensor upgrades. #21743. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
  • Sources indicate that the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
  • Revision, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

Sources indicate that the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Revision, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and mentioned that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

It has been revealed that each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Sources indicate that parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Industry observers note that secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were swiftly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

It has been revealed that as noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

According to recent reports, last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher stated he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

It has been revealed that the blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that meta’s executives are rethinking the firm’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
  • According to recent reports, the firm’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
  • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that meta’s executives are rethinking the firm’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

According to recent reports, the firm’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the tech giant’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and Fresh Hampshire. The tech giant attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

It has been revealed that for comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Massive Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing newly introduced renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

According to recent reports, but even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Industry observers note that still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

It would very much be in the public interest for other Massive Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

It has been revealed that google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

According to recent reports, the other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

According to recent reports, it’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s newly introduced AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that highlights that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

In a recent development, this change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

It has been revealed that super Agent uses OpenAI multimodal models and Realtime API to enable tasks across text, image, and voice, allowing people to automate complex workflows with simple prompts, no coding required. The system took off: in just 45 days, Super Agent reached $36M in ARR, driven by strong user demand.

Genspark initially introduced as an AI search engine designed to help consumers and professionals synthesize and structure information. By late 2024 user behavior started shifting. Users didn’t just want answers. They wanted outcomes. Instead of “summarize this market,” they were asking for pitch decks, video scripts, and follow-up emails. At the same time, model capabilities were rapidly expanding. Longer context windows, stronger reasoning, and upcoming multimodal APIs made it increasingly possible to automate entire workflows, not just retrieve information.

That shift in user demand and model readiness led the team to make a bold move: in April 2025, Genspark pivoted away from search and fully embraced agentic AI.

In a recent development, in April 2025, Genspark launched Super Agent: a fully autonomous, no-code assistant that can make phone calls, design slides, generate videos, and more. Under the hood, the platform orchestrates nine specialized large language models and more than 80 integrated tools, dynamically assigning each task to the best-suited component.

It has been revealed that openAI models are central to this system. GPT‑4.1 handles research and structured outputs with improved instruction following and a 1M-token context window, allowing agents to process long documents in full without truncation. Strict JSON output is designed to ensure reliably structured responses for downstream tools, while automatic prompt caching reduces latency and API costs which is especially valuable in multi-step workflows. For image generation, the platform uses the GPT‑image‑1 model via the OpenAI API.

Because the system is fully no-code, consumers don’t need to think about any of that. They describe what they want, “call my dentist,” “summarize this report,” “make me a slide deck”, and Super Agent handles the rest.

One of Super Agent’s most talked about features is Call For Me, an AI that makes real phone calls for you, and actually holds a conversation. No scripts. No clunky transfers. Whether booking a reservation or rescheduling a delivery, the agent uses the OpenAI Realtime API and speech-to-speech capabilities to handle the conversation naturally and with real-time fluency.

In a recent development, A dual-layer system powers the interaction: the Realtime API manages the live dialogue, while a shadow model monitors and guides the interaction via message queue. The result is fast, coherent back-and-forth, even when the call includes hold music or ambiguous human responses. In Japan, one use case went viral: owners asking the agent to handle resignation calls to their employers. It’s the kind of deeply human interaction most people don’t expect an AI agent to handle.

Beyond phone calls, customers rely on Super Agent to create personalized content. Ask for a vaporwave-style pitch deck, and the agent drafts the slides, generates stylized cover images with GPT‑image‑1, and compiles the final deck. For video, it can write a scene-by-scene script, generate the images, and assemble an Instagram-ready short.

Recent findings suggest that these use cases are possible by OpenAI multimodal capabilities, Genspark’s execution speed, and their close collaboration with the OpenAI startups team. Genspark met regularly with OpenAI solutions architects to share best practices, fine-tune workflows, and optimize model performance. They were among the first to launch voice experiences with the Realtime API, and continue to contribute feedback that helps drive model improvements.

In a recent development, “We chose OpenAI not just for model performance across modalities, but for developer experience,” claims Zhu. “The OpenAI API design helped us move promptly, shipping, debugging, and scaling without bottlenecks.”.

In just over a month after launching Super Agent, Genspark has:.

Grown to $36M ARR in just 45 days.

Shipped eight major agent features in 70 days.

All of this was achieved with a 20-person team and no paid advertising. That growth was entirely organic, driven by product virality and word-of-mouth. Much of Super Agent’s appeal comes from its accessibility. People don’t have to build workflows or configure settings. They just say what they need and the agent handles the rest.

Next, Genspark is expanding into upcoming categories where autonomous agents can drive even more value, like an AI browser that acts on all of the content you’re browsing and AI docs for generating format-rich documents. OpenAI APIs remain core to how the team builds fast and ships faster.

In a recent development, “We built Genspark to be more than a chat interface, it’s an all-in-one AI workspace,” says Zhu. “And with OpenAI APIs, we were able to make that real in record time.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI joins the American Federation of Teachers to launch the National Academy for AI Instruction.
  • It has been revealed that for educators, AI can be a powerful ally, helping free up more time for the truly human work of teaching.
  • Now is the time to ensure Al empowers educators, students, and schools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI joins the American Federation of Teachers to launch the National Academy for AI Instruction.

It has been revealed that for educators, AI can be a powerful ally, helping free up more time for the truly human work of teaching. Recent Gallup study⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) showed that 6 in 10 educators are already using an AI tool and report saving an average of six hours per week. But it also raises new challenges: how to ensure AI enhances rather than bypasses teaching, and how to help students foster critical thinking when answers are instantly accessible.

Now is the time to ensure Al empowers educators, students, and schools. For this to happen, teachers must lead the conversation around how to best harness its potential.

It is for this purpose that we join the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) as the founding partner for the launch of the National Academy for AI Instruction, a five-year initiative to equip 400,000 K-12 educators, about one in every 10 teachers in the US, to use AI and lead the way in shaping how AI is used and taught in classrooms across the country.

In a recent development, as the first partner to pledge support, OpenAI is contributing $10 million over five years—$8 million in direct funding, and $2 million in in-kind resources including engineering support, computing access, and technical guidance to help teachers build and use AI tools in real classrooms. OpenAI is joined by the United Federation of Teachers, Microsoft, and Anthropic in supporting the initiative. Our shared goal is simple: to support teachers in shaping, using, and guiding the development of AI in K-12 education.

These investments will help establish a flagship facility in Fresh York City and support the launch of additional hubs around the US by 2030. The Academy will serve as a national hub for free training and curriculum, combining real classroom expertise with cutting-edge technology. The Academy will also fund and deliver professional development opportunities that prioritize equity, accessibility, and measurable impact in K-12 education.

Over the next five years, the Academy will:.

Support over 400,000 educators across the US in developing practical AI fluency by 2030.

Offer workshops, online courses, and hands-on training sessions.

Prioritize broad access and tangible benefits, especially in high-needs school districts.

Launch a flagship campus in Fresh York City, and scale nationally.

Through OpenAI’s support, educators and course developers will get:.

Priority access to OpenAI’s technology and future tools designed for education.

Tokens and API credits to build custom, classroom-specific tools that support educators.

Technical support to integrate AI tools into the Academy’s learning platform and into schools’ learning systems.

Pictured: Michael Mulgrew, President of UFT; Randi Weingarten, President of AFT; and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, signing an agreement to launch the National Academy for AI Instruction on June 10, 2025.

“Growing up in Saint Louis, my high school computer science lab is where I first got curious about AI—mostly thanks to an incredible teacher who pushed me to experiment, even if I broke a few things along the way. Educators make the difference, and they should lead this next shift with AI. We’re here to support them.” —Sam Altman, Co-founder & CEO, OpenAI.

In a recent development, “AI holds tremendous promise but huge challenges—and it’s our job as educators to make sure AI serves our students and society, not the other way around. The direct connection between a teacher and their kids can never be replaced by latest technologies, but if we learn how to harness it, set commonsense guardrails and put teachers in the driver’s seat, teaching and learning can be enhanced.” —Randi Weingarten, President, AFT.

According to recent reports, this initiative builds on our ongoing work between OpenAI and AFT to support free and accessible tools for educators and help them lead the way in shaping how AI is used in the classroom. It also builds on OpenAI’s work to make our tools more responsive to real academic needs⁠. Additional existing resources available to educators include the OpenAI Academy⁠(opens in a new window), ChatGPT for Education⁠(opens in a new window), and the OpenAI Forum⁠(opens in a new window).

OpenAI is also the proud co-sponsor of the upcoming AFT AI Symposium to be held July 24 in Washington, DC.

For more information about the National Academy for AI Instruction, please visit www.aft.org⁠(opens in a new window).
